explanations.explanation: That's the word the LORD uses. He says to deal with “…one who sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s commandments…” (Leviticus 4:2). This is the sin you didn't mean to do, like sitting on your own sunglasses. You never saw it coming, but it still counts. Notice the LORD makes a way for it anyway.

Anger isn't in this message, friend. The LORD says this is about someone who sins unintentionally (Leviticus 4:2). Nobody here is slamming a door or stomping around the camp. This is the sin that sneaks up on a person.

Pride doesn't show up in this message. The LORD says it's about someone who sins unintentionally (Leviticus 4:2). Nobody is puffing out their chest here. The text says unintentionally, so that's the word I'm sticking with.

Right there in the text: when the anointed priest sins, he is “…bringing guilt on the people…” (Leviticus 4:3). The priest's sin, and the guilt lands on the people. That's a lot of weight for one pair of shoulders. It's like a delivery guy who trips on the porch step and the whole box of cookies goes down with him. His stumble isn't just his.
The text says it reaches further than that. The anointed priest's sin is “…bringing guilt on the people…” (Leviticus 4:3). His sin doesn't stay in his own tent. It lands on everybody he serves.

His household isn't mentioned here. The text says the anointed priest's sin is “…bringing guilt on the people…” (Leviticus 4:3). So the guilt reaches a lot more folks than the ones at his dinner table.

explanations.answer: When they become aware of the sin
explanations.explanation: That's the timing: “…when they become aware of the sin they have committed, then the assembly must bring a young bull as a sin offering…” (Leviticus 4:14). Becoming aware is the cue the verse gives. No calendar needed for this one.

explanations.answer: On the next day of rest
explanations.explanation: The text sets no day like that. It says “…when they become aware of the sin they have committed…” the assembly brings the bull (Leviticus 4:14). The trigger is knowing, not the calendar. Nobody gets to say 'I'll circle back on this one.'

explanations.answer: At the end of the year
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't hold it until the end of the year. The assembly brings the bull “…when they become aware of the sin they have committed…” (Leviticus 4:14). Becoming aware is the trigger the verse names. The end of the year isn't mentioned anywhere in it.

That's them: “The elders of the congregation are to lay their hands on the bull’s head before the LORD…” (Leviticus 4:15). The elders are the ones the text names for the hand-laying on the assembly's bull. Then it shall be slaughtered before the LORD.

The Levites aren't named in this part of the passage. The text says the elders of the congregation lay their hands on the bull's head before the LORD (Leviticus 4:15). The elders are the ones who stand for the assembly here.
Judges don't appear in this passage. The text says the elders of the congregation lay their hands on the bull's head (Leviticus 4:15). That's who stands up for the assembly in this moment.

Close, but the elders have a different job. They lay their hands on the bull's head (Leviticus 4:15). The one who makes atonement is the priest: “in this way the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). So the statement is False.

Yes, it's False. The elders lay their hands on the bull's head (Leviticus 4:15), but they don't make the atonement. The text says “…the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). Everybody has a part, and nobody takes somebody else's job.

That's the word: “…the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). Look at where the verse ends up. The assembly is forgiven. I'd hang that one on my bakery wall.

That word isn't in the verse. It says “…the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). No surprise inspection waiting at the end of this one. The verse closes on forgiven.

Scattered isn't how the verse ends. It says “…the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). The offering ends with the assembly forgiven, not sent running in every direction.

True. The text says “When a leader sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the commandments of the LORD his God, he incurs guilt.” (Leviticus 4:22). Unintentional or not, the leader incurs guilt. The passage then says he brings an unblemished male goat when he becomes aware (Leviticus 4:23), and the priest makes atonement and he will be forgiven (Leviticus 4:26).

It's True, friend. The text says a leader who sins unintentionally “incurs guilt” (Leviticus 4:22). Having a title doesn't change that. The good news is that the leader gets an offering and forgiveness too (Leviticus 4:26).

explanations.answer: A pleasing aroma to the LORD
explanations.explanation: The priest burns the fat on the altar “…as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.” (Leviticus 4:31). Then comes the next part of the verse: “In this way the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven.” So the aroma goes up to the LORD, and the one who brought the goat is forgiven.

explanations.answer: A warning to the whole camp
explanations.explanation: No warning here. The text says the fat is burned “…as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.” (Leviticus 4:31). That's the purpose the verse gives, and it's all about the LORD. After that comes forgiveness for the man who brought it.
The elders don't get this one. The fat is burned on the altar “…as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.” (Leviticus 4:31). It goes up to the LORD, and nobody in the camp takes it home.

True. The text says “If, however, he brings a lamb as a sin offering, he must bring an unblemished female.” (Leviticus 4:32). At the end of the lamb's steps it says, “In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:35). Goat or lamb, the forgiveness is the same.

It's True, friend. The text lets him bring an unblemished female lamb instead (Leviticus 4:32). And with the lamb it says “…the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:35). Same forgiveness as with the goat.

True. The text says that touching something unclean, “…even if he is unaware of it, he is unclean and guilty.” (Leviticus 5:2). The verse says he's unaware of it. It's like finding a smear of dough on your sleeve you never saw. It was there the whole time.
It's True, friend. The text says “…even if he is unaware of it, he is unclean and guilty.” (Leviticus 5:2). Not knowing doesn't take the guilt away. That's why the LORD gives a way to be made right.

It's False, friend. The text says if someone swears thoughtlessly “…to do anything good or evil…” then “…when he realizes it, he is guilty in the matter.” (Leviticus 5:4). Good or evil, a careless oath still counts. So a good-sounding promise doesn't get him off the hook.

Yes, False. The oath can be “…to do anything good or evil…” and “…even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty in the matter.” (Leviticus 5:4). Words said in a rush still count. Think twice before you promise.

That's the word: “If someone incurs guilt in one of these ways, he must confess the sin he has committed…” (Leviticus 5:5). No dodging and no 'mistakes were made.' Confess is the word the LORD uses. Then he brings his guilt offering to the LORD (Leviticus 5:6).
Mourn isn't the word in the verse. It says “…he must confess the sin he has committed…” (Leviticus 5:5). Confessing means saying it plainly and owning it. After that comes the offering.

Nobody's keeping a ledger in this verse. It says “…he must confess the sin he has committed…” (Leviticus 5:5). Confess is the word the verse uses, and recording isn't in it. After that the offering comes (Leviticus 5:6).

It's False, friend. The text says, “If, however, he cannot afford a lamb, he may bring to the LORD as restitution for his sin two turtledoves or two young pigeons…” (Leviticus 5:7). The verse doesn't make him wait for a lamb. It gives him another offering to bring.

Yes, False. The text says that if he cannot afford a lamb, “…he may bring to the LORD as restitution for his sin two turtledoves or two young pigeons…” (Leviticus 5:7). A small budget doesn't shut the door. The verse gives him another offering to bring instead of waiting for a lamb.

explanations.answer: Because it is a sin offering
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives: “He must not put olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.” (Leviticus 5:11). The verse does the explaining for me, and I love it when that happens. Nice work, baker!

The text gives a different reason. It says “He must not put olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.” (Leviticus 5:11). The remainder of the flour does belong to the priest (Leviticus 5:13), but the oil and frankincense are left off for the reason in verse 11.

explanations.answer: Because the oil is for the lamps
explanations.explanation: Lamps don't come up here. The text says “He must not put olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.” (Leviticus 5:11). That's the whole reason it gives.

The text says “In this way the priest will make atonement for him for any of these sins he has committed, and he will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 5:13). Any of them means the silent witness, the unclean touch and the careless oath. The flour covers the same sins as the lamb. A small offering, a full forgiveness.

That's too small. The text says the priest makes atonement “…for any of these sins he has committed…” (Leviticus 5:13). That includes the silent witness and the careless oath too. The flour isn't limited to one.

That's too small. The text says the priest makes atonement “…for any of these sins he has committed, and he will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 5:13). That reaches past the oath to every sin on the LORD's list. One handful of flour, and the whole list is covered.
